title: Distributed Key-Value Store (DynamoDB / Cassandra Style)
summary: A system design case study of a Dynamo-style distributed key-value store: partitioning with consistent hashing, replication, quorum-tunable consistency, conflict resolution, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy and gossip-based failure detection.

chapters.title: Distributed Key-Value Store Cover
points: Problem and scope
Requirements and scale
High-level architecture
Partitioning and consistent hashing
Replication and quorums
Conflict resolution
Hinted handoff and anti-entropy
Gossip and failure detection
Scaling and interview questions

chapters.title: Problem, Scope and Requirements
points: Scope: put(key, value) and get(key) on values up to 400 KB; no joins, no multi-key transactions, no secondary indexes in v1
Functional: put, get, delete (tombstone), per-request consistency level (ONE, QUORUM, ALL)
Scale estimate: 10 TB hot data, 1M reads/s plus 200K writes/s, 100 nodes, ~100 GB per node
Latency targets: p99 read under 10 ms, p99 write under 15 ms; availability 99.99%
Non-functional: always-writable (AP by default), horizontal scale, no single point of failure, incremental scalability
CAP stance: during a partition choose availability and reconcile later (eventual consistency)

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture (Distributed KV Store)
points: Peer-to-peer ring: every node is identical, no master, any node can act as coordinator
Request path: client → any node (coordinator) → N replicas → ack when quorum met → respond
Per-node stack: coordinator layer, membership/gossip layer, storage engine (commit log + memtable + SSTables)
Client-side vs server-side routing: smart clients cache the ring and skip one hop; otherwise a proxy forwards
Replication factor N=3 across 3 availability zones is the default deployment

chapters.title: Partitioning with Consistent Hashing
points: Responsibility: map each key to an owner node with minimal data movement when nodes join or leave
Design: hash(key) with MD5 or Murmur3 onto a 2^128 ring; owner is the first node clockwise from the key's position
Naive hash(key) mod N moves ~(N-1)/N of keys on resize; consistent hashing moves only ~1/N
Virtual nodes: each physical node owns 128-256 tokens, which evens load and lets stronger machines take more tokens
Flow: adding node D takes tokens from neighbors and streams only those ranges to D
Data model: token map (token → node), per-node range list, partition key plus optional sort key
API: getPreferenceList(key) returns N distinct physical nodes; skip vnodes of the same host or rack
Failure: hot partition from a skewed key (one celebrity key) is not fixed by hashing; salt the key or cache
Metrics: keys per node (skew under 10%), streaming bytes during rebalance, hottest-partition QPS

chapters.title: Replication and Preference List
points: Responsibility: store each key on N=3 nodes so data survives node and zone loss
Design: coordinator plus the next N-1 distinct nodes clockwise form the preference list
Rack and AZ awareness: replicas placed in different zones so one zone outage loses at most 1 of 3 copies
Flow: coordinator sends write to all N in parallel, waits for W acks (not sequential chain)
Data model: key, value, version metadata (vector clock or timestamp), tombstone flag, TTL
Failure: a replica down for hours is covered by sloppy quorum and repaired later; permanent loss re-replicates from peers
Metrics: replica lag, under-replicated ranges, cross-AZ bandwidth

chapters.title: Tunable Consistency with Quorums
points: Rule: R + W > N guarantees a read overlaps the latest successful write; N=3, R=2, W=2 is the standard
Settings: W=1 fast-write, R=1 fast-read; R=1,W=N read-optimized; R=N,W=1 write-optimized
Read flow: send read to N, return after R responses, pick the newest version, read-repair stale replicas in background
Write flow: coordinator timestamps or versions the write, sends to N, returns after W acks; latency is the Wth-fastest replica
API: per-request consistency level (ONE, LOCAL_QUORUM, QUORUM, ALL); LOCAL_QUORUM avoids cross-region latency
Failure: R + W > N does not give linearizability; concurrent writes and sloppy quorums can still return stale data
Metrics: stale-read rate, quorum failure rate, p99 latency per consistency level

chapters.title: Conflict Resolution: Vector Clocks vs LWW
points: Vector clock = list of (node, counter) pairs; version A descends B if every counter in A ≥ B's
Concurrent versions (neither descends) are kept as siblings and returned to the client for merge
Example: D1[(A,1)] then write via A gives D2[(A,2)]; concurrent writes via B and C give D3[(A,2),(B,1)] and D4[(A,2),(C,1)], which conflict
Last-write-wins stores a timestamp; highest timestamp wins, no siblings, simple and used by Cassandra
LWW drawback: clock skew of even 100 ms silently drops a legitimate write
Vector clock drawback: clocks grow with writers, so truncate at ~10 entries, and the app must merge (for example shopping cart union)
Choose LWW for idempotent overwrites; choose vector clocks or CRDTs when losing a write is unacceptable

chapters.title: Failure Handling: Hinted Handoff
points: Responsibility: keep writes available when a preference-list replica is temporarily down
Sloppy quorum: write goes to the first N healthy nodes on the ring, not strictly the first N
Flow: stand-in node stores the write plus a hint naming the intended owner, then replays it when the owner returns
Data model: hint table (target node, key, value, version, created_at) with a TTL of ~3 hours
Failure: if the stand-in dies or the hint expires, the write is lost on that replica and only anti-entropy repairs it
Metrics: hints stored, hints replayed per second, hint backlog age

chapters.title: Anti-Entropy with Merkle Trees
points: Responsibility: find and fix replica divergence that read repair and hints missed, without scanning all data
Merkle tree: leaves hash key ranges, each parent hashes its children, so the root summarizes the whole range
Flow: two replicas compare roots; if equal they are in sync, else descend only into mismatching children and sync those leaf ranges
Cost: sync cost is O(differences · log n) instead of O(n) data transfer
Data model: one tree per token range per node, rebuilt periodically; ~64K leaves per tree is typical
Failure: tree rebuild is I/O heavy and range membership changes on rebalance invalidate trees
Metrics: repair duration, bytes streamed per repair, ranges not repaired in over 10 days (must stay under tombstone GC grace period)

chapters.title: Gossip and Failure Detection
points: Responsibility: decentralized membership and liveness with no central coordinator
Gossip: every 1 second each node exchanges state with 1-3 random peers; information spreads to all nodes in O(log N) rounds
Data model: per node a heartbeat counter, generation, status (UP, DOWN, JOINING, LEAVING) and token list
Detection: a node is suspected when its heartbeat has not increased within a timeout; phi-accrual detector outputs a suspicion level, with phi above 8 marking DOWN
Seed nodes bootstrap new members and prevent split gossip clusters
Failure: network partition makes both sides mark the other DOWN; a false positive triggers needless hinted handoff
Metrics: gossip convergence time, flapping nodes per hour, detection time under 10 s

chapters.title: Storage Engine and Write Path
points: Responsibility: make local writes fast and durable on each replica
Write flow: append to commit log (sequential disk) → insert into in-memory memtable → ack
Flush: memtable at ~128 MB flushes to an immutable sorted SSTable on disk
Read flow: check memtable, then SSTables newest-first, with a Bloom filter (~1% false positives) skipping files lacking the key
Compaction merges SSTables and drops overwritten values and expired tombstones
Failure: crash recovery replays the commit log; deletes need tombstones kept past gc_grace (10 days) or deleted data resurrects

chapters.title: Scaling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions
points: Scale out: add a node, it takes tokens from neighbors, bootstrap streams ~1/N of data, no downtime
Trade-offs: N=3,R=2,W=2 balances latency and consistency; AP gives availability but exposes stale reads and siblings
Comparison: Dynamo is leaderless with vector clocks; Cassandra is leaderless with LWW; Spanner-style stores use Paxos leaders for strong consistency
Common mistakes: LWW with unsynced clocks, too few vnodes causing skew, never running repair so tombstones resurrect
Interview Q: what happens if 2 of 3 replicas are down at QUORUM? (write fails, unless sloppy quorum or ONE)
Interview Q: how do you add a node without a reshuffle? (consistent hashing plus vnodes)
Cheatsheet: N=3, R=2, W=2; ring via Murmur3; gossip 1 s; hints 3 h; Merkle repair weekly
